rounds.text: HP Adhesives Ltd currently exhibits a profound disconnect between its market valuation and its underlying operational performance. The company trades at a P/E ratio of 132x [E1], which balloons to 174.25x when compared against a sector benchmark of 21.06x [E6], while the EV/EBITDA multiple of 35.08x significantly exceeds the sector benchmark of 12.25x [E11]. This optimism is fundamentally unsupported by the business results, as compounded sales growth is -4% [E14] and compounded profit growth has plummeted by -85% [E15]. Furthermore, the operating margin has collapsed from 13% three years ago to 2% in the trailing twelve months [E20], and the company’s institutional support has evaporated, with foreign and domestic institutional holdings dropping to near-zero levels [E33, E34]. Conceded: the company maintains a conservative debt-to-equity ratio of 0.02x [E28] and has successfully backed its profits with cash [E24]. Despite these balance sheet strengths, the stock’s negative momentum, evidenced by a -31% three-year share price growth [E16] and a negative Sharpe ratio [E46], suggests that the market is pricing in an unrealistic 37.3% earnings growth rate that the current operational trajectory cannot justify [E38].

The bear’s focus on high multiples like the 132x P/E [E1] and 35.08x EV/EBITDA [E11] ignores that the company is currently positioned for a recovery within a sector experiencing a strong tailwind [E67, E68]. While the bear highlights recent profit declines [E15], it overlooks the most current evidence showing that earnings growth is already accelerating [E61], with both sales and profits showing improvement on a quarter-over-quarter basis [E59, E60]. Conceded: the operating margin has faced pressure [E20, E21]. However, the company’s financial foundation remains rock-solid, as it is almost debt-free [E51] with borrowings reduced by half over the last year [E30] and a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.02x [E28]. The bear’s claim that the market is pricing in unrealistic growth [E38] ignores that the stock is trading at a price-to-book ratio of 1.71x, which is actually a discount to the sector benchmark of 1.85x [E7]. Finally, the assertion that institutional support has evaporated [E33, E34] fails to acknowledge that promoters maintain a significant 71.35% stake [E32], signaling strong internal confidence in the business's long-term viability.

The bull’s reliance on a sector tailwind [E67, E68] is disconnected from the company’s actual performance, as HPAL’s compounded sales growth is -4% [E14] and profit growth is -85% [E15], significantly lagging the sector’s median sales growth of 17.9% and profit growth of 34.0% [E69, E70]. While the bull points to accelerating growth [E61], this is contradicted by the yearly operating margin trend, which has been decreasing for four years [E22], and a quarterly operating margin that plummeted to -1% in Jun 2026 [E21]. Conceded: the company is almost debt-free [E51] and has reduced borrowings [E30]. However, this conservative balance sheet does not justify a P/E of 132x [E1] or an EV/EBITDA of 35.08x [E11], which remain vastly higher than sector benchmarks [E6, E11]. The bull’s focus on the P/B ratio [E7] ignores that the stock’s intrinsic value is estimated at only Rs 5 [E36], resulting in a massive -589.1% margin of safety [E37]. Finally, the claim of internal confidence via promoter holdings [E32] is undermined by the exit of institutional investors [E33, E34] and negative money flow [E35], which align with the stock’s -31% three-year price decline [E16].
